name: Spot the craft failure
note: Five interview moments. The technical content is fine in every one — diagnose what the candidate's craft is costing them before revealing.

items.prompt: A candidate reads the system-design prompt, says "okay, give me a minute," and works silently on the whiteboard for six minutes, producing a correct architecture. What did those six minutes cost?
candidates: Everything the interviewer can grade: silence is indistinguishable from being lost, the reasoning and trade-offs never became visible, and the interviewer can't steer toward what they wanted to assess
Nothing — correct architecture is the only deliverable
A few style points, recoverable with a good summary
The whiteboard marker dried out
items.correct: Everything the interviewer can grade: silence is indistinguishable from being lost, the reasoning and trade-offs never became visible, and the interviewer can't steer toward what they wanted to assess
items.explanation: Communication failures are the most-cited rejection reason — one published review of ~50 hiring decisions put them at ~40–45%, and practitioner guides consistently rank them first, ahead of any knowledge gap. The interview's actual product is your visible reasoning: narrated structure, trade-offs spoken as they're weighed, checkpoints that let the interviewer redirect. A silent right answer scores like a guessed one.
items.principle: Think aloud structurally: narrate the plan, the options, and the choice — the reasoning IS the deliverable.

items.prompt: In an AI-assisted coding round, a candidate prompts the assistant, gets ~200 lines, pastes them in, runs the tests (green), and says "done." The interviewer asks why a particular helper function handles the empty case the way it does. The candidate doesn't know. How is this scored?
candidates: As a failure — the round assesses verification and comprehension under automation; shipping code you can't explain or defend is the named anti-pattern, green tests or not
As a pass — the tests are green and that's what tests are for
As neutral — the assistant wrote it, so the assistant defends it
As a pass if the candidate offers to refactor it
items.correct: As a failure — the round assesses verification and comprehension under automation; shipping code you can't explain or defend is the named anti-pattern, green tests or not
items.explanation: AI-assisted rounds (Meta and Canva have shipped versions; Google has announced its pilot) grade four things: strategic prompting, genuine code comprehension, verification-and-debugging, and communication while automating. Relying solely on prompting is an explicit fail condition. The visible failure mode even has a shape: 200 pasted lines, a feeling of productivity, and nothing you can defend — failing while the code looks fine.
items.principle: You own every line you ship, whoever wrote it. Review and verify like the author you now are.

items.prompt: Same round, different candidate. Before touching the AI, they say: "My theory: the bug is in the pagination offset; I expect the fix in fetch_page, and this failing test should flip first." Then they prompt. Why does this beat diving straight into prompting?
candidates: They preregistered a falsifiable theory — now the AI's output gets checked against a prediction instead of accepted on vibes, demonstrating governance over the tool rather than dependence on it
It doesn't — it wastes a minute the AI could have used
It's mainly politeness toward the interviewer
It guarantees the AI gives a better answer
items.correct: They preregistered a falsifiable theory — now the AI's output gets checked against a prediction instead of accepted on vibes, demonstrating governance over the tool rather than dependence on it
items.explanation: Committing to a theory — which files, which invariants, which test flips — before invoking the assistant turns its output into evidence for or against your model of the system. If the AI's fix lands somewhere your theory didn't predict, that's a signal to understand before accepting. The alternative gets derided as 'prompt theater'; this is the durable skill that survives every tool version.
items.principle: Preregister, then prompt: commit to what you expect so the output can actually be verified.

items.prompt: Asked "how would you tune HNSW parameters for this workload?", a candidate who has never tuned HNSW says: "I haven't tuned HNSW specifically — here's how I'd approach it: it trades recall against latency, so I'd benchmark recall@10 on our golden set across ef_search values against the p95 budget." Strong or weak?
candidates: Strong — an honest gap, immediately bridged with the right structure (the trade-off, the measurement, the constraint); this is what transfer looks like under pressure
Weak — admitting any gap is disqualifying at senior levels
Weak — they should have improvised parameter values confidently
Neutral — the interviewer will just move on
items.correct: Strong — an honest gap, immediately bridged with the right structure (the trade-off, the measurement, the constraint); this is what transfer looks like under pressure
items.explanation: Bluffing specifics gets probed and collapses; bare 'I don't know' leaves points on the table. The bridge pattern — name the gap, then map the unseen thing onto a structure you do own (here: a tunable trading recall for latency, measured on a golden set against an SLO) — converts every stretch question into a demonstration of how you'd learn. That mapping skill is trained, not innate: it's what every chapter's stretch problem was for.
items.principle: Bridge, don't bluff: name the gap, then map the unknown onto a structure you own.

items.prompt: Behavioral round: "Tell me about an AI system you shipped." The candidate gives a fluent two-minute story — problem, approach, launch — with zero numbers: no scale, no metric movement, no cost, no eval result. What's the gap?
candidates: Unquantified impact: without baseline → intervention → measured movement (and how it was measured), the story is unverifiable narrative — and overstated impact without metrics is a screening failure hiring managers explicitly cite
The story was too short
Behavioral rounds don't expect numbers
The candidate should have name-dropped the model vendor
items.correct: Unquantified impact: without baseline → intervention → measured movement (and how it was measured), the story is unverifiable narrative — and overstated impact without metrics is a screening failure hiring managers explicitly cite
items.explanation: The strongest behavioral answers about AI systems are eval stories wearing a narrative: here's the metric that defined success, the baseline, what I changed, what moved, and how I knew the movement was real (the same golden-set discipline as Chapter 5). 'Deflection went from 31% to 47% on a 400-ticket golden set, holding junk-answer rate flat' survives any follow-up; 'it worked great' invites one.
items.principle: Quantify the story: baseline, change, measured movement, and how you measured — or it didn't happen.
